utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, ma'am. Amongst the accused I notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic. Ms. Nikolic, I understand he's not feeling well today? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. And he has an appointment with his doctors and he's given us his oral approval or waiver for his right to attend his trial, and I expect that we will get the written document in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. I appreciate that. So we can proceed. Prosecution today is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Mitchell. The Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Josse, and that's about it, I think. Yes. I understand, Mr. McCloskey, you also have a preliminary?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly, Mr. President, and good morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- everyone. As you are likely aware 22 October a Miletic and Pandurevic filed a motion asking that a witness be changed from -- to go public. And we have no objection to that, and we would like just to have you waive any requirement in filing and any response just to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So, while usher is bringing in the witness, let's make things clear. We are determined to finish with the testimony of this witness today. There is no way we will let you keep this witness here during the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you had a good rest. We are doing now our utmost to finish your testimony today so that you -- sorry. My apologies to the interpreters I had my mic off. So good morning, Mr. Simic, we are trying to do our best to finish our testimony today --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- so that you can join your family as soon as possible. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when we interrupted your cross-examination, I was asking you whether in your visit to Srebrenica you passed by the DutchBat base in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes I did pass by that base --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The counsel and witness are kindly reminded to make pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw what the base looked like and where it was situated between the city cemetery and it seems to me a gas station. That would be its approximate location. It was to the right of the road, if you're looking in the direction of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to see whether there was any damage caused by shells or any other damage to the base or the area in front of it, to the building itself mainly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see any damage. What I did notice were the sandbags or whatever it was used to make those military shelters or whatever you want to call it. They were all around the base. They had been set up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, did you by any chance have an opportunity to revisit Srebrenica in that period? I am now referring to July 1995 after the first visit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, several days later or after the evacuation somebody called me and asked me if I could receive and take somebody to Srebrenica, a senate or a congressman either from Britain or from America, and he wanted to go to Srebrenica to just go through at this time, to walk through it and to drive through it. That's what he wanted, and that's what I did. I went there with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you had an opportunity to observe what the situation was like in Srebrenica in detail and to show this foreign national?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that we walked from the town centre, and he went wherever he pleased. I did not instruct him at all. He went to all the parts of the town that he wanted to visit, and I merely escorted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what was your impression after that visit? Were you now able to better observe the state of the town?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because the first time I drove through I was in a car and now I walked the streets together with him. We didn't see any broken glass, any rubble, any kind of damage that you expect to see in a town after fighting. And as I said, that's something that I didn't notice even the first time when we just drove through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, in your testimony in the Blagojevic case you mentioned that when you were at Potocari you had seen some of your students, some of the people you knew from Srebrenica and that you spoke to them. Do you remember speaking about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and this is something that will remain indelible in my memory. It was a touching meeting for me, I was moved; and to tell you the truth I was afraid of meeting somebody because I would have felt uncomfortable in -- about meeting them in a situation in which they were in a difficult situation. But yes, I do remember quite clearly meeting those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in contact with those people from Srebrenica, did any of them complain to you about the shelling, about being exposed to the shelling as civilians or exposed to any kind of abuse by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't tell me anything to that effect. They didn't mention any kind of abuse or anything of the sort. The only thing they complained, this female student of mine told me that she was happy that the day had finally come for her to leave Srebrenica, and she was sorry that she couldn't do that earlier because most of her family was out of Srebrenica and she was alone there. And she told me that life in Srebrenica had been very hard on her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. I don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. McCloskey. Can you give us an idea how long you will be cross-examining this witness so that we know whether to keep the next witness or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I certainly hope to do it within two hours and I'm trying to keep my record of less than an hour, but you just never know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A little deja vu, we've been here before.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, your direct testimony and my excellent cross-examination is already in the record, so we'll try to avoid some of that -- or most of it if we can. Let me ask you a couple of issues of -- related to some of the things you did see. Do you remember seeing when you were in Potocari on the 12th this rush for the buses by the Muslims and Muslims trampling each other?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you did see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think you also said the Muslims actually left some people behind, got on the bus and left their family behind; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who couldn't walk, they had carried them to the buses and then they left them in front of the buses, near the buses, and got onto the buses leaving them behind. And then I carried those infirm people into the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you had to carry the Muslim family members because they wouldn't do it themselves?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't just look at those infirm disabled people who were just sitting there looking around, and those were mostly women as I've already indicated. You could see that they had been disabled since birth, and I tried to stop people, telling them whose family member is this woman? Why are you leaving her behind? Things like that. But they just went on. And then I picked those people up and carried them into the buses, and I put them onto the seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you stand by everything you said in your previous testimony, let's be clear on that. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you -- what are now your immortal words, you said on page 7612, after describing your the testimony the food, the bread that was brought to the crowd: "The food was a drop in the sea, I must say. I was surprised when I realised what the situation was. I had never seen anything like it. It was shocking and remained shocking to me to this day." You stand by those words?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, about the food. Let me -- I want to read you something short that is in evidence in this case from a Dutch witness named Koster. His testimony came in at 65 ter 2269. And he said: "Well, we escorted the Major Nikolic with our liaison officer and an observer, and he walked down through the people. After that, he returned and also saw the situation, stayed the same for a couple of hours, probably, then one of the commanders came to my position and told me that he would bring a vehicle, loaded with bread for the people and that we should make way for this vehicle. And it really appeared -- and then they started to give bread to the people. They also had a camera team accompanying them, and the camera team, well, they were filming while they were giving bread to the people." So did you see that camera filming when the bread was being handed out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it goes on and says: "And how many people did get the bread? Did they have something for everybody?" Answer: "No, not at all. There was a very small truck, and well, they were throwing the bread and giving the bread to the people. My interpreter told me while they were doing that they were shouting at the people again and mocking them and calling them names." So while you were around the bread being handed out, did you -- did you hear the people handing out the bread calling names and mocking people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. Simic. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could question just have a page reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's ERN 01038916, page 38 of Koster's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So was -- did you hear all that, the mocking and the calling the comments that --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, I don't know who drove that truck with the bread, and I heard the people who had come in from Ljubovija invite the people, telling them, Come in, come here, take the bread. And since this was further away from the buses, I carried the bread there, and I didn't notice anyone calling anyone names. Actually, I wanted the people who had brought in the bread to distribute it because that was their contribution to all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we've heard evidence in this case from a Corporal Groenewegen, page 2973 of testimony I'm sure we all remember of testimony from 25 of October, 2006. Question: "You also said this was filmed by a Serbian television, a TV crew that came together with a Serbian soldiers, do you recall that?" Answer: "Yes I do." And you also said that: "When the film stopped filming this distribution of bread that they continued to distributing the bread to refugees?" "Yes, that's correct." So having that in mind do you still recall no -- no filming of the bread?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it must have been -- well, somebody must have distributed that bread before I came, and it was not the bread distribution that I took part in. Because when I got there, I really didn't see any cameras filming. Well, I cannot deny that, that there was somebody there, but I didn't see anyone there up there with the camera. And I was not really interested in any cameras. If somebody had been filming I would not have paid any attention. However, I do not recall having seeing a camera at Potocari while I was there. And it was sometime between 1300 hours, so if this distribution was done before 1300 hours, then I was not present there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, let me go over just briefly and confirm some of the things you say you didn't see. You've just testified that when you went to Potocari -- when you went to Srebrenica on the 12th and later you saw no bodies. Surely, you've seen the famous film that's been played over and over again of the walk that Mr. Kovac and other made through Srebrenica on the 14th of July that shows, I believe, three to four dead Muslims in a gutter with a dog around it. I won't play that for us. We've seen that plenty of times, but you've seen that film, haven't you? Shot by a Serbian journalist?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. I only saw what you mention now, the camera that filmed the first meeting [as interpreted] between Mladic -- or with Mladic, and I saw that Ljubisa Borovcanin was there, that was the first time that I saw it. The first contact with the people who had gathered at Potocari; and to this day that's the only footage that I had seen. And the next day they showed me some military unit that had come in from Sarajevo, but I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I am informed that the word "meeting," page 10 line 4, not the correct word. The word that the witness used is "encounter."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. There is a difference, of course. Do I have a confirmation of that from someone, the interpreters in particular? Page 10, line 4, in the transcript we have, "in the first meeting with Mladic." Mr. Gosnell is saying that the word used by the witness was "the first encounter" between Mladic or with Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat the word that he witness used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you please, Mr. Simic, repeat the word that you used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my reply to which answer, if you could just specify that, because I leave this kind of thing behind me and now I have to revisit this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Anyway, shall we move, Mr. Gosnell? All right. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, sir, I just want to confirm, and this will be very brief, I hope, that despite the fact that you tell us you were in Potocari for several hours on the 12th witnessing the clamoring on to the buses. Today, as you sit here, you are standing by your conclusions that you saw no separations of family members, of male family members, you saw no abuse, no beatings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I told you what I had seen, I repeated that several times, and now I don't have the right to say things that are not correct. I cannot change the way I see things. I can see why you might think that this is strange, but that's just the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday, when you were being asked questions about this encounter with someone that you -- someone later told you was Mr. Beara, you said: "I did not have any visual capabilities at all," and you talked about the blood rushing to your eyes or something. Can I take it your visual capabilities for Potocari were okay?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably at the beginning, yes. But later, as I have the habit of saying I said my impressions of all of that began and then they intermingle the past, the present, and the future. So I don't have any capabilities that somebody else in my place would have to notice what was going on. I intermingled three tenses, so -- at the time so that image was not only visually shocking, but it meant to me the past that I had with those people; it wasn't bad. And the present, the situation in which the people happened to be. And what will happen in the future, after all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go on to a different subject, and that is you've testified about Kravica at length, and the story you heard; and I want to just again confirm that this is correct in your testimony, Blagojevic at 7629: "I heard about that the following day. Not the day when it happened. And the story that I heard, was that a policeman who was guarding those people in the Oka; and I don't know how they came to be there, whether they were brought or they had come on their own, that that policeman was killed and then shooting started. Or shooting ensued. And I heard about this from returning soldiers."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if you're following the transcript, that is one of the adjusted parts of the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like this. I will help you to understand this better --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I don't --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so Mr. Nikolic in the morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am just asking, you can explain it if you need to. But are you standing by that testimony? Yes or no, and you may explain your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now that my friend at the end has given permission to the witness to actually respond, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Let's proceed. Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, do you stand by the statement, and you can always explain your answer.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do stand by my statement, and I wish to explain what it means and how all this came about. After Nikolic's story that we heard in the morning hours, in the course of the day the soldiers who were returning from the lines or whatever they were, I don't know where they were deployed; they were coming back from that direction of Kravica, and they passed by Oka; and they were saying on the street already that something had happened. They had seen that they were killed in front of the Oka and they wanted to see what had happened. They were asking around if anybody knew what had happened up there. That is why I said -- that is why I was mentioning soldiers in that sense, because they were sitting in buses, the buses were going, they didn't stop there. They saw through the windows of the buses because Oka is not far from the main road that Kravica-Konjevic Polje road or the Kravica-Bratunac road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So the story that you say you heard was that first a policemen was killed by one of the Muslims, and then the people responded; the Serbs responded and killed many of the Muslims. That's the guts of the story, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the story that I heard, probably Nikolic heard it from somebody up there. I don't know from whom. And that is the story that we heard from him, and that's the only thing that we knew at that time. Up to now, I haven't heard anything new.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we now know, and I don't think there is an issue, that in fact a -- a Serbian MUP officer did burn his hands on a rifle that a Muslim had used to kill Serbian -- Serbian MUP and an army member. And so I don't think that's contested, but what I want to ask you about is if you heard this story in a little different way; and I want to show you a brief clip of a video to emphasize my point and to help you remember what you may have really heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is Exhibit P02047. It's just the short Kravica clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Starting at 02.56.57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I would just like to know how the playing of video clip is actually going to assist witness with what he heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps he should take off his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, can you remove your headphones, please. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the Prosecution's position that Mr. Simic would have heard precisely what had gone on at the Kravica warehouse. He would have heard accounts of what we now have on the video, and my point is directly related to what we see on the video. And my question is exactly on point towards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. Let's proceed. Mr. Simic, can you put your headphones on again, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, what this will be, sir, is Mr. Borovcanin has told us, which I don't believe is contested, that he is -- he is heard over the radio that a member of his unit -- or that there is a problem, and he goes quickly to this area where the problem is; and he's got this guy with him that's filming it. And this guy, Petrovic, happens to film this little section that we see at the time that Mr. Borovcanin arrives to this horrible scene; and so you're going to see that film that Mr. Borovcanin has rushed to this terrible scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not having any sound, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am -- sometimes that happens with sanction. I hope we get sound, because it's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. That's why I pointed it out. It follows what you just said from a couple of minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Nothing as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have an ongoing problem with this particular software. It's haunting me. Mr. President, I -- I don't want to waste anymore time. I think -- I don't think that it's contested that we see this video. It comes to one side of the warehouse, as it gets to the end of the warehouse, and right before it goes black you hear automatic weapon fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we are going to go back and do a slow motion and freeze it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is the front of the Kravica warehouse. It's not contested that those are bodies piled there. That Mr. Borovcanin is arriving quickly to the scene of the warehouse. And I can tell you that there is evidence in this case that inside the warehouse there are many hundreds of people; and it's the Prosecution's position that at this time they're dead or disabled or dying. Now, Mr. Borovcanin is arriving suddenly to the scene where one of his officers has been wounded. Wouldn't the story that you would have heard, if it was the correct story of what happened, wouldn't it have been Serbian armed forces began executing people, began shooting people in this warehouse halfway through those executions when these men in front of you are dead and dying; a Muslim comes out of the crowd, grabs a gun, and shoots it. And that's when Mr. Borovcanin gets the word to come. Isn't that the story you heard? That this thing had been halfway through before the Muslim grabbed the gun and killed the Serb? Isn't that the real story?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is something wrong. I can hear him speaking but -- okay. It's the microphone that got cut off. Can you repeat, Mr. Simic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the Prosecutor is saying is something that I'm hearing for the first time. I didn't hear this story from anyone else. I have no evidence or material that is available to the Prosecutor. I cannot speculate on that. I told you what I had heard. I cannot say that I had heard something else or that I found out something else. What the Prosecutor is saying now is something that I am hearing for the first time. He probably has his own reasons why there is this story, why it exists, if it exists. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, we'll go on to some documents now and hopefully a little less difficult topics. In your testimony in Blagojevic you spent a fair amount of time in 1992 and Morillon and other historical issues which I don't want to get into in detail, but I do want to go back there a bit. And you had told us that were the president of the municipal assembly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you in June of 1992 a member of the war commission?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was not a member of any commission, or I don't have any idea what sort of a commission this would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You weren't on it with Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but you don't know about the creation of the war commission?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Maybe it's a translation issue, and let's just go to the document and see if you can help us with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 3837. It's a document dated 16 June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we have here pursuant to the decision of the presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the establishment of War presidencies, and it goes on and talks about this war commission. And there is five people, you're not listed there, but we do see that you signed this thing. So you would have known about this, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature. I did sign it, but this was probably a long time ago and I signed it -- I mean, I signed a lot of things and I really cannot recall every single thing to which I put my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, now that you see it I'm sure it brings back some issues. This was a decision from the presidency. That's -- we're talking, I don't want to get into the presidency in 1992 but it certainly involved Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I give my comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that these members of the War Presidency, I don't know how this exactly went, but I'm not familiar with it, but in case a state of war is declared, then in a state of war the assembly would not be functioning and then this war commission then or whatever it is would be working. At least that is what I believe. I am not absolutely sure, but I think that it was some sort of preparation so that we wouldn't be taken by surprise if war broke out within the municipality with such a situation. But I think the assembly was still functioning because I signed it, so this was a precautionary measure in case a state of war was declared, then the municipal institutions would be functioning in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So now you do recall the establishment of this war commission?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that it is the 16th of June, 1992 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So my question is -- so you now looking at this now remember the establishment of this war commission and your involvement?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't participant. I don't know how it was established. This was just brought to me for signature because as you can see in the heading it's the Republika Srpska and not the municipal assembly. This is probably done by the republican commissioner who was signed on the left side. I was not in a position to establish a War Presidency, neither did anybody authorise me to do that. Perhaps the president did this through his commissioner, and that commissioner signature is at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This refers to you as president of the Serbian municipality of Bratunac. It doesn't say president of the assembly. Is this thing right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, this -- you can see we were just wondering around in the beginning, and in the heading it says, "Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbian Municipality of Bratunac." All these municipalities had the same Srpska in their name to indicate -- I don't know their what. I mean, it's wasn't even that clear to me why it's just the municipality of Bratunac; but it's the Serbian municipality of Bratunac; it is some sort of decision of the Republican parliament or the government. I don't know. We received instructions to make stamps in that way, and that is what we did. Our stamp bore that title. I couldn't decide how the municipal stamp would look or what the assembly would be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not concerned that you're calling yourselves the Serbian this or the Serbian that. I don't want to get into the nationalism that may or may not be behind that word. That's not the word I am asking you about. You said you're the assembly guy, this says that you're the president of the municipality. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Serbian municipality. This is correct that I am the president of the assembly, and I said that in Bratunac up until it will reforms of the local assembly, there was no chief nor was I any kind of president in the sense that I was a chief or a mayor. These abbreviations of titles in speech frequently happened also in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're not on trial here. We're trying to get an -- I'm trying to get an idea of whether or not you are going to be able to tell us credible information. So that's why I am asking this. You're not on trial, but if you think you are going to say anything that may implicate yourself, you don't have to talk; but let's go to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a document 65 ter number 3813.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I want to give a hard copy of this because it's kind of long. And I'm really not interested in the substance of it, but I just want you to help me with a couple of these titles that we seem to see. This is a -- we've seen this in Court before, I think with the last person. This is a document dated August 27th of 1992, some sort of inspector named Sasa Blagojevic from the Serbian Ministry of the Interior from Sarajevo it looks like -- comes -- it looks like he's doing some sort of inspection on the police station. Your name gets mentioned in here, but what I want to ask you about is -- it's a reference it's on -- in your copy it's the last paragraph on page 2, in the English it's part of the last paragraph on page 2. And it says: "After all these talks which were held at the Bratunac SJB, we agreed on a meeting with representatives of the army and the municipal government, which was attended by the president of the municipality Ljubisav Simic; the chairman of the SDS party, Miroslav Deronjic; the war commission, Tesic; on behalf of the municipality, Colonel Dimitrije Sibanic; and Staff Sergeant Drago Nikolic on behalf of the army; head or chief of the SJB Luka Bogdanovic; commander of the police station, Ljubomir Borovcanin; deputy chief, Branimir Tesic; and head of the criminal department, Budimir Lakicevic." So just having that in mind let me just start with a couple of other questions. You said that in 1992 you were a member of the SDS party, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the key figures in government in the police have to be members of the SDS party in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police did not belong to any party, but it's a fact that the parties that were in a majority in the assembly provided proposals for the posts of chief or commander. They couldn't appoint either the chief or the commander but would their opinion on the candidate that would be proposed by the assembly or the SDS; and then that would be decided on at a higher level, ministerial level. I mean, he could not have perhaps received support and somebody else would have been appointed instead; but they would provide their opinion on candidates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And for example the chief of the SJB Luka Bogdanovic, was he a member of the SDS party in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not -- at least I waited a little bit, but we are not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, we not get the interpretation. Let's try again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could start again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The question I asked was --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I think that the microphone is not working again, ah, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So my question was -- if you could just start over.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that as I already said and it wasn't heard that the commander and the chief of police could not have been elected by anyone at the municipal level, neither the party nor the municipal government or the municipal assembly. A proposal could be put forward which would be made by the majority party in the parliament, they would pass that proposal for candidates probably to the ministry, I mean, I don't know I didn't directly take part in that. Miroslav was the period of time of the party told know that better, and the proposal could have been either accepted or rejected. Those people, as candidates were not members of the party, any party as far as I am aware. They were never considered to be a candidate of our party or their party, but it would mean that perhaps our proposal would be accepted, would pass, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I am not asking whether they were a candidate of one party or a member of -- of some party organisational body. I am just asking are they a member of the party, you know, do they --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the answer is no. But the president may have kept records of that, but I am not aware of any of them or either of them being a member of the party. Well, let me clarify this, I did not have any function in the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But Bratunac is a small town, you're going to know who is a member of the SDS and who isn't in 1992, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that we were all in favour of removing politics from the army and the police. That had been our objective right from the start. The army and the police were not there to be involved in politics but to do their job. I know that we all advocated that approach and this is something that I welcomed right from the start, because I always was bothered when I saw the army officers sit in the front row at the assembly session, the police officers in the second row.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I agree that you would be concerned that if Ljubomir Borovcanin was a member of the SDS as a police officer or a chief of police you would be concerned that he may be acting in conformance with some of the goals of the SDS as opposed to some of his police jobs, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not something that would concern me because we didn't instruct him what to do. He received his instructions from the ministry. Even if he had been my brother, he would have had to do things not the way I tell them but in accordance with the laws and regulations of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you helps, looking in this document, just past the part I read to you, it mentions at the meeting the SJB chief gave a short overview of the activities that had happened in Bratunac; and then it, which we know from this document was this guy, Luka Bogdanovic, and then after that it says, "The commander of the police station proposed a solution to the volunteer problem," et cetera, and we know that's Ljubomir Borovcanin. Can you tell us what's the difference between the head of the SJB and the commander of the police station?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Excuse me, it may not be obvious to the witness what time-period we are talking about. So perhaps if that could be specified in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The time-period in this document, 1992, 1993, time-frame. And if it changes, let us know.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. I will tell you this, and I will have to disappoint you because quite frankly I don't know that. I am a layperson, I don't know anything about the structure of the police. I knew that there was a commander and there was a chief; and I thought the chief was superior to the commander, "komandir," and I thought the chief ordered the komandir how to organise work, what to do inside the police station; and I never walked into a police station before the war, during the war, after the war. I only went there to get documents on official business, so I never really studied the internal structure; and I didn't think that it was my job to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I don't need details on the internal structure, but the SJB chief, is that the superior to the -- what the transcript --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Komandir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we have the Bogdanovic is the superior of Borovcanin in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a higher post than the komandir, that's all I can tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, if you keep looking down this document, eventually this inspector says what you say, and I'm not -- I don't think I need to read it all but basically we can see that the president of the municipality, Ljubisav Simic, pointed out there were a loft flaws regarding the organisation of the three government levels on its territory, emphasizing that also members of the security services were engaged in illegal actions. It goes on to talk about police admitting that in this matter there are a lot done already and that the police should be engaged especially in preventing -- so clearly, your job, you know all about the police and the different government levels. You're advising inspectors from Sarajevo about it, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't talking about the situation inside the police. When I said "all three levels," I wanted to say that in every segment of the government there are people who do their job badly, and on the basis of my experience with the police work; for instance, when I went to work or went back home, and as I passed through the municipality I observed the policemen; and we could see that even for a long time after the war that there were some policemen who had not been trained to do their job properly. And I always criticized that wherever I could whenever I could I criticized that kind of behaviour. And if this inspector had come in to hear my opinion, I felt that it was incumbent upon me to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if Mr. Borovcanin was ever a member of the SDS during his time in Bratunac in 1992, 1993, and 1994?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that because I didn't look at the records of their membership. I wasn't interested in who was the member of the party. I joined the party because I was persuaded to do that, not out of any great love for the party. So I never really was interested in who was a member, who became a member. I knew about the members who were already there, some of them, and I was not interested in who was joining the party later. And to this day, I don't know whether Borovcanin was a member of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shouldn't have been possible for him to have been one, but he was then it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I think we can go on. Did Mr. Borovcanin get promoted to the chief of the SJB? Did he get Bogdanovic's job eventually?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall whether military rule in Bratunac in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me. There was talk about declaring a state of war often, and rumors were circulating in the army ranks that some kind of military rule would be established. But as far as I can recall, the state of war was declared at the very end of the war. So the army could not impose any kind of rule. They were trying to do some other things, they would mobilize people and call them up and just send them to the front line, all of us, myself including; and then we would be there for two or three days, and then we would all be allowed to go back. They claimed that there was some kind of an imminent danger. We were all complaining about that, and Miroslav himself also presented those problems that we faced through his chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, were you part of a command for military rule in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any kind of military rule or command where I would perform some kind of a task or role.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you a member of the military rule from the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 3838 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would the witness please be asked to take his headphones off?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Simic, can you remove your headphones, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour, this is an entirely fair line of questioning. I would simply suggest that the wording used is a little bit ambiguous, and so I would object to the ambiguity; and if there is a precise organ or institution that's being referred to then that should be put to the witness first before there is a move to impeach him based on the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I take it Mr. Gosnell finds objection to the use of the term "military rule" and would like that be to be clarified or to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I'll show him a document that it says: "After informing them about the situation, the command of the military rule, headed by brigade commander is coordinator of all activities in the municipality was established. The following persons are appointed to the command of military rule" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, no, let's proceed. At that point in time if it's a phrase that has been used in a public document, we can proceed. And in any case, I was noticing that the witness had answered the previous question making reference -- to which reference to military rule was also made, and let's proceed. Mr. Simic. Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I just want to clarify. I apologise, could the witness please be asked to take the headphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, could you remove the headphones again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I do believe that I am informed that the there is a translation issue. And that the word that's being used in the document that may not be a correct translation, at least into English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. One moment, is he going to be shown the document in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if they are not going to object -- we have a standing objection, they don't like us reading the documents. Yes, he is, I have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So there is no problem. If he is going to see a document in B/C/S there is no question of mistranslation. So let's proceed, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, we all hope we have a translation issue here and not a perjury issue. But let me show you the document I am talking about, and maybe we can clear it up. I have got a hard copy for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 3838.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am sure you can clarify this for us. Maybe it will help refresh your recollection. Go ahead and take a little time to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we get the -- well, I take it the Court has the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So take your time. We see this. It's from the Bratunac brigade command, dated 30 December 1992, to the Drina Corps command. It makes reference to an order issued by the president of the Republika Srpska on 29/12/1992, establishing of military rule in the Bratunac municipality. And it says: "After informing them about the situation, the command of the military rule, headed by the brigade commander as coordinator of all activities of the municipality, was established. The following persons are appointed to the command of the military rule: President of the municipality, Simic, Ljubo; for assistance, Lieutenant-Colonel Kuljanin, Ranko; for cooperation with the MUP, Major Savcic Milomir; Second-Lieutenant Popovic, Jovo; Borovcanin, Ljubisa, commander of the police; and others." I will ask you again, sir. Were you part of the command of the military rule that was created in December 1992 in the Bratunac municipality? And you do not have to answer if you think it is going incriminate you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me explain to you before you answer what Mr. McCloskey is trying to tell you. We have a rule here that if any question is put to you which if truthfully answered by the witness could possibly expose him -- expose you in this case to incrimination, then you have a right to ask the Trial Chamber to exempt you from answering such a question. The Trial Chamber is free to exempt you or not to exempt you, but if it forces you to answer the question, then whatever you say here, provided you don't perjure yourself, cannot be made use of any criminal proceedings that I may be instituted against you. I hope you have understood, if you need more explanation we are here precisely to do so. Otherwise, if you wish to answer the question, please proceed to answer it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Simic, let me just preference the question with context. December 12th, 1992, is just a week before Kravica Christmas. We know that the forces of Naser Oric, the 20 -- well, the forces of Naser Oric whatever they were back then, had had significant gains, threatened Bratunac, that Bratunac was in deep trouble; it needed help from Serbia, you were in military rule. So I am just asking you, sir, are you a member of that military rule group to deal with this horrific situation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that it occurred in this matter that it is described in this document and the way you put it to me. I remember that the situation among the people was such and all the blame was shifted to us in the municipality. I don't know how we were able to do anything to prevent this in Kravica and to calm down the people, because passions were running high. Then somebody used this situation as a pretext saying that we --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- we were standing in the way of the army --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- it was a simple question, do you now remember being in part of the command of the military rule?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was Ljubisa Borovcanin a member of the military --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're [Realtime transcript read in error, "yes"] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. He's answered it anyway, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, we've now been in 1992 for about an hour, I believe, and it's legitimate to inquire into matters concerning the credibility of the witnesses. It's not legitimate if we're going into other matters, this is nowhere near the scope of the indictment, so I object on that ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I take it -- we are. Let's proceed, let's proceed Mr. McCloskey, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I will remind counsel that his testimony is full of 1992 which he put in evidence. The Vuk Karadzic school --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure I got an answer, do you know if Ljubisa Borovcanin was a member of the military rule, then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could use this term every time when somebody from the command invited us to come in the critical moments because they always invited me, the president of the executive board, and somebody from the police. Because, of course, those structures, at critical moments, demanded that a joint solution be found for any problems that existed in in the area where we lived. So that I think that for all intents and purposes this was never implemented. It was just a meeting where it was decided what to do to calm down those people in Kravica who had been through this calvary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. There is a reference -- a correction of the transcript that I think is essential to be made now. It's at line 10, page 31. The witness apparently did not say "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In mine it will be line 12 and not line 10. So that needs to be attended to. I don't think it's important at this stage. You've just pointed it out, but the question was put again and answered later on. So we don't have to worry about it. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I will just go on if that's all right. I can try to clear that up or you can clear that up. I would have doubted that he would have said yes, myself. But I think I will go on to the next situation. Now, sir, do you know if there was a no confidence vote against Luka Bogdanovic by the SDS? You've talked about this process of recommending people. Back in February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Luka Bogdanovic was invited to a session of the assembly to notify the deputies about the situation in the municipality and the deputies pose some questions. He, I guess, was the chief at that time; and the deputies were not happy with his answers, and I know that this lack of confidence and dissatisfaction with his work was expressed by the assembly. And then I'm sure that the party, because it had the majority, had to send this dissatisfaction and non-acceptance of the report to the ministry or whoever was in charge of personnel decisions at the level of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, let's go to 65 ter number 210.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I hope not to spend too much time with this document, and it's minutes from the Bratunac SDS municipal board held on 1 February 1993. Did you go to the SDS -- were you part of the SDS municipal board?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were part of the SDS main board?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, hopefully we can just take a look at this, the minutes, the part I am talking about is page 20 in the B/C/S, and it's also page 20 in the English. And it -- let me know if you remember this happening. You see these three numbered paragraphs on this page -- in fact, let me give you a hard copy because this -- the machine is hard sometimes. But it says here in one that there was "A no confidence vote in the chief of the public security service was carried out by the main board with 18 votes against and three restrained ..." and that basically they wanted to take measures to replace Luka Bogdanovic, and the main board nominated Ljubisa Borovcanin, who currently works as the commander of the ... do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's clear we're not now dealing with impeachment. I renew my previous objection. We are outside the scope of the indictment by a long way. There is no material facts coming close to this subject matter, so question object to these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The documents that he has in evidence go into 1992, the person's position, his description, he talks about the Vuk Karadzic school incident of 1992, the shipping out of people in 1992. Mr. Ostojic went into quite a ways of who was a member of the SDS and who was not. These issues are so far open, and they are important issues that I think the Court needs to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the relevance of the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He has earlier testified he doesn't remember whether or not Mr. Borovcanin was replaced Luka Bogdanovic and now here's a document to refresh his recollection or impeach him. Given his testimony it could be either one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's a legitimate question. Mr. Simic, if you could answer the question, and then we'll go to break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as you can see the main board at the republican level was in charge of personnel issues not at the municipal level. And this initiative on the part of the assembly was then taken to that level and the decision was made there. As far as I can recall, Luka left to some post in Zvornik after that. And now whether Borovcanin was the chief or not, I don't know, because believe me it was not my task, and I didn't like to deal with that. This was Deronjic's task to deal with the personnel issues. It was not in my jurisdiction. He was the president of the party, president of the deputies club, and this was his job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We have to stop here. The break will be of 20 minutes, not the usual 25, and during the next session I will be absent because I have an urgent bureau meeting, so we will be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. I'll join you later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a preliminary. It concerns some elements of the cross-examination that has just taken place. I understand that some of the propositions that have been put forward by the Prosecution are new. They hadn't previously been part of the Prosecution case, and I believe that we are entitled to ask what the Prosecution position is in respect of these particular elements. And I would like to now tell you what the three elements are. First, we would like to know whether it is the Prosecution's position whether Mr. Borovcanin was the chief of police, the chief of the SJB, in Bratunac at any time. Second, we would like to know if it's Prosecution position that he was a member of the SDS at any time. And third, we would like to know whether the Prosecution is alleging that he had any duties in Bratunac before August 1992. All three of these matters were raised or put forward as propositions by the Prosecution, and we believe we are entitled to know what their position is on these matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, regarding number 1, whether or not Mr. Borovcanin was the chief of the SJB, I have been trying to sort that out with this witness based on his testimony; the testimony that's in evidence, some of the documents we have. And perhaps at the end of his cross-examination, we will know more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So meaning that you are -- you don't have that -- you don't have your case in relation to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All I've seen so far in the documents is the SDS wants to dump Bogdanovic and replace him with Borovcanin. I don't have any documents showing that that replacement happened right now. I think this man knows; I don't know if he will tell us, and I think they know. But this is all coming up in response to these witnesses, and, frankly, the opening statement. When they get up and say that Borovcanin comes into Srebrenica on 11 July as a guy that doesn't know anything about what happened before that, and to me this is a fairly outrageous part of their Defence. And so we are responding through their witnesses to that and to the documents and to the issues that are brought up, the SDS, the memberships, the police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could keep your answer just to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, he's asking the position of the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What about the second point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A member of the SDS, I have documents that show he is a member of the SDS and that this person is involved and that's coming. And where he was -- what he was doing in August of 1992, I have my suspicions but I don't know. At this point I don't know. Does that help?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. The third point was, whether he had any duties, responsibilities, in Bratunac before August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Same answer. I don't know. We may find out if -- through these witnesses these folks that know all about 1992 and get asked about 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I really don't think this is proper then. Essentially what we have is a fishing expedition in case the Prosecution doesn't have a case on these points. They are just fishing around trying to find something prejudicial. It's not within the scope of the indictment; it's not within the scope of the pre-trial brief. I think that these matters are out of bounds. Actually, we do know that all three of these allegation are unfound, that's the important position. But the more important point is that these matters are beyond the scope of the indictment, they are beyond the scope of the Prosecution indication, and essentially they are muck raking, and we don't think it's proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it not arise from the questions and answers and contents of the documents spontaneously? Can you not think in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, as I tried to make a record, we don't object to the questions on credibility that go back to that time-period, but we do object to the questions that are being put in order to incriminate Mr. Borovcanin from that time-period. So I believe our position is consistent on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- thank you. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can I respond to that last one very previously?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This cross-examination has been specifically organised so that it would respond to what was brought up by the Defence. When they offered in his testimony from the other trial where he's talking about 1992, about Morillon, the Vuk Karadzic school; and then we go in -- Mr. Ostojic goes into, you know, who is a member of the SDS, who is not. The first few questions of this witness which were absolutely appropriate and fair have led to these other issues which are in response to the issues prosecute up by the Defence. This is an organised cross-examination based on the evidence that is before us and what the Defence has done. This is not a fishing expedition. They have asked me, generally, about issues not really related to the cross-examination. Before August 1992? I haven't gotten into that. I don't know where that comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that the issues relating to 1992 were brought up by the Defence in direct, and in cross by the Defence, so the Chamber will allow the Prosecution to continue. But we are not sure how relevant they are, so if you could proceed in a more expeditious way. Having said that, could we bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you remember in January 1994 that Ljubisa Borovcanin indicated his desire to join the SDS board?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 210. And B/C/S, I see it's page 37. I've got the handwritten minutes of the meeting that may be able to be helpful for the witness. English, I think it's page 41, and B/C/S is first part is page 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, these are minutes, handwritten minutes, as you can see, from the meeting of the Bratunac SDS to the Serbian Lands Municipal Board held on 18th January, 1994 at the Hotel Fontana. You've told us that you were a member of that board. And if we go down, under, well, it's on the bottom of the first page in English. It starts off under number 1: "The president, Miroslav Deronjic, presented material from the main board ..." and it goes on for a while. And then the part I want to show you, and it's underlined, Miroslav. It says: "Consultations with certain people are already taken place regarding their joining the board, and those people have accepted membership. So far the following people have stated that they would want to join the SDS board: Petar Loncarevic, Veljko Malesic" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the page for B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's either page 37 or 38 in the B/C/S. I'm not exactly sure. If you can find the Miroslav ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "... so that the people that want to join the SDS: Loncarevic, Malesic, Ljubisa Borovcanin, Slobodan Ilic. Talks remain to be held with ..." and then it lists some other folks. So you were a member of the board back then, do you remember this? Does this help refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say this is 1994, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The minutes say that this meeting happened in 18 January 1994 at the Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really must say that I don't remember this. I don't deny it happening, but I really don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So these -- these minutes look genuine to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say this is Miroslav's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So they look genuine to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the document is still in handwriting, so I couldn't really say. And probably later it was sent for typing and certification. This is done in some kind of notebook. It's probably a draft minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, did you know that Miroslav Deronjic was -- or someone was taking notes like this for the SDS municipal board meetings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would do it for himself. As presiding, he had to make some sort of sketch or improvise minutes for himself so that he could conduct the meeting in a sequential way. There was also a minute-taker who was the minute-taker of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that it's Deronjic's. I am not sure. I think that is how he writes. If I would be able to get something about which you are sure that is his or that I am sure that it is his, then I could compare that and then I could be sure. Like this, it's difficult to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It says the minutes are taken by Mirna Nikolic. Is that the person you are talking about that takes the minutes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that she was the minute taker. I think she was the secretary of the SDS and that she was the one to take the minutes at these meetings; but if she happened to be absent then somebody from those present would be entrusted with taking the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who's Mirna's husband?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him. I know that she got married, but I don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Her husband?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I don't know, I don't have a clue. You're the Bratunac expert.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe if it's the second wife of Momir Nikolic. As far as I know, he was married; and he worked at the school together with me for a while and he had a wife and children. Mean, if this is his second marriage then, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's one subject I don't need to get into. Let's go now to see what happens, we've got February 1994 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 210, page 45 in the English, page 40 in the B/C/S. This one is another handwritten one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me give you that just so that you've got that one too. Try not to get them mixed up. This one begins as we see in the -- from the Bratunac SDS board meeting held on 17 February 1994, (Thursday), in the small hall of the people's university with the beginning at 1600 hours: "Out of the 37 board members attended the meeting, also present were the members who need to enter the board, Ljubisa Borovcanin, Petar Loncarevic, Nedjo Milanovic." Do you remember that looks like the first time that Ljubisa Borovcanin actually came to a meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't remember those present but it's possible. Members who were being admitted. Now, the procedure before that, again I am talking about work that I was not carrying out, so I cannot speak in anymore detail about that. But I know that the practice was that a candidate that was being put up should come to the board so that the other members would be persuaded that really is their wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this look like the same handwriting that you saw before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you think it's Miroslav's handwriting, not Mirna's?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure, but since I am reading it easily and in this part I was able to read Miroslav's handwriting without any difficulty. On the basis of that, I think that it could have been his, perhaps it's Mirna's. I never certified her minutes or read them, so I am not familiar with her handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, you should look on page 40 of the Serbian -- page 46, it says Miroslav underlined again. And the English says: "For the co-opt of the new board members, he nominates Radisa Jovanovic, Fakovici local board; Stojan Ilic, Bjelovac local board; Nedje Mladenovic, local board, Repovac; Ljubisa Borovcanin; Petar Loncarevic; Slobodan Ilic; Nedjo Milanovic; and Momo Peric." So is this the Ljubisa Borovcanin -- sorry, I'm almost done by the way. Is Ljubisa Borovcanin in the minutes of this SDS meeting the same Ljubisa Borovcanin that is in court today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know two people that have that same name in Bratunac. I don't know of another Ljubisa Borovcanin other than this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what's the answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then these are the minutes who was invited to the municipal board, but this, about these names that you read, it seems to me that things like this in the SDS were present in 1995. As for 1994, it's not quite right to me. And this is why I believe that because elections were coming up. And probably the party was getting ready for the election, and it was looking for new members and wanted to know what cadre and what membership it could count on. I see that it is 1994 here and activities of the party from 1994 to this extent that these were preparations then; although, it was possible. I don't have that in my memory, but I know that more extensive activities in 1995/1996 were conducted to register membership and new parties, beginning to be formed and the party had to know some members of ours that had entered the assembly had transferred to other parties and then we had to make a record once again of who actually was a member and who was not. That is what I know about those activities. Well, roughly, because I did not conduct the immediate party policy. This was something that was done by Mr. Deronjic and that was his more important part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So these minutes support the conclusion that on 17th February, 1994, Ljubisa Borovcanin and the same Borovcanin in this courtroom was elected as a member to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I really don't know. Looking in these minutes I am seeing for the first time that Ljubisa Borovcanin was invited to the board that he was proposed. I didn't read to the end whether he was voted in, did he become a member of the SDS. I didn't hear that as a sensational item of news, so that I would be able to recall it subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I am just asking you the to look at this document. It says that --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says here on the 17th of February, 1994. I don't recall meetings like that; it's possible that they did take place but I have no memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, you can't get water from a stone. The witness has answered the question, and the document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For you enough. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am sure that they wouldn't have called a stone to the witness stand. I will read it if I have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The part I didn't read, if that's okay, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where it says that: "Miroslav's nomination was unanimously adopted." Doesn't that mean he was a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection, the witness has indicated he doesn't have any additional knowledge about these -- he's indicate his state of knowledge, which is he doesn't remember this and all other inferences are based on the document which we can all read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is does this document indicate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because witness said that he didn't read to the end, so I will allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was -- thank you, Mr. President that was my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am now reading it to the end, you are reading it to the end; it says, "Miroslav's nomination was unanimously adopted." Doesn't that mean that Borovcanin is now a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what I know, it should have been voted on; and it should have been confirmed at the municipal board. I don't know if this had to be revised by the main board afterwards or reviewed by the main board. I said that this was not the job that I was usually doing, and I did not enter the infrastructure of the party in order to remember this as something -- as some important event. It was not an event for me. It could have been an event as far as Miroslav was concerned, because he was the one who took care of the party about the quality, composition of the membership in the party, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
