utterances.text: Okay, one more question about this and I'll go on and not this subject. Did -- at the time of this document, February 1994, if Mr. Borovcanin is the commander of the police of Bratunac, would he have been required by the political situation by the realities at the time? Would he have been required to be a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state with full responsibility no. Ljubisa Borovcanin would not have been more or less capable of doing the job that he was already performing had that been the case. But look, this is 1994. Ljubisa Borovcanin, according to my knowledge, left Bratunac -- I don't know whether it was in 1993. He led some sort of special police unit and probably his status was not the same. I believe that Miroslav had made inquiries about that. Again, I said that I was not able to do that, that was his job. If he, as commander of some sort of special unit that did not have the status of a policeman, did have or didn't have, I am guessing now. Perhaps the best thing would be for me to stop speculating now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good idea. So if we can conclude then if he was not required to be a member of the SDS in 1994, that if he was a member in 1994, he did it on his own volition. Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. McCloskey -- no, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps he ... I would like to so that it's clearer to the gentleman. I don't want to deny him. I think that it's possible that Mr. Borovcanin planned to withdraw from the police and that he could be counted on as a man who could be assigned to one of the positions. Perhaps that could be the reason for you to understand more easily why Ljubisa Borovcanin expressed a desire to enter the SDS so that he could become the SDS cadre. But this had nothing to do with the police functions. With that he could perhaps later be assigned or appointed to some civilian function. I think, perhaps, it is clearer to you now so why he is appearing in these minutes from 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, let's go to another document. It may clear up some of these things. 65 ter 3840.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to go to the Bratunac Brigade command and get into the gate without having to go through all the normal ID hassles and things?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't able to. I had to stop at the gate or the reception area where the officer on duty was. I don't know exactly what their name was, but it was a soldier. I had to give my ID card. I had to be searched to show that I wasn't carrying any hard materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But did they have your name at the gate so that when you showed up they would treat you accordingly to your position that you deserved?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably they had the name, but they checked. Not all the people who were there knew me. I mean, think changed shift. They couldn't all know me, especially because in Bratunac from 1992 onwards the structure of the population changed and the indigent population quickly became the minority population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well let's just take a brief look at this document which is dated 20 January 1994. And it's an army document from the commander at the time, Slavko Ognjenovic. It's entitled, Regulation for the crossing, the reception of the command of the specified persons. It just says: "The duty officers with the reception of the brigade will without further delay in the brigade command permit crossing of the following persons." Miroslav Deronjic and Ljubisav Simic are the first two people. We go down it a ways we see some familiar names, Jovan Nikolic, Luka Bogdanovic, who is the chief of the MUP at that time; and now we see Ljubisa Borovcanin, commander of the MUP. So do you remember now? Does this help refresh your recollection that unlike what you've just said about when he might have left that Ljubisa Borovcanin was in fact the commander of the MUP on January 20th, 1994 was still around?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just is a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very difficult to intervene.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell. Now, your objection will be moot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must say there might be a translation issue. I just want to make sure we are using the right terminology and distinguishing between number "7" and number "8." That's the only comment I would like to make in respect to that last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think the witness has tried his best to explain all this -- JUDGE KWON yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- and I don't think there is anything more that we need to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin told us that he, I believe, left in February of 1994. Does that seem to make more sense to you than what you said earlier?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you quite clearly. Could you please simplify your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, in looking at this document and its date --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- and taking it as a truthful statement that Mr. Borovcanin told the Office of the Prosecutor that he left in February -- February 24, 1924 [sic] -- February 24th, 1994, does that help refresh your recollection about when he was there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does that sound about right to you, from your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, really, even when I said it I never asserted that I knew when he left. I noticed later that he wasn't in Bratunac and that I -- and I heard that he had went to take up some other duties, I think in Bijeljina. As for these dates here, they probably confirm that; but still the explanation that I got earlier is that it's possible that Ljubisa Borovcanin was planning to leave the police and to wait for some kind of solution to change his profession, and you can ask him that. I, myself, didn't ask him that. And as I said, he wasn't within my area of sight. As some member who would come to the SDS, I know definitely that if he had joined the SDS he would have had to be relieved of his duties in the police. He would have had to do that today. Had he become officially a member then he should have said -- or he would need to say I am no longer working in the police, please find some other solution. I mean -- but this is something that he would have needed to discuss with Deronjic. I don't know what I discussed with Deronjic. He definitely did not discuss anything on that subject with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So he was close to Deronjic, Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he was close or not. If he wanted to join the party and change his job, then he had to approach him and talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, just one last short area and a few questions. You, in your Blagojevic testimony, you talked a fair amount about the events of 1993, General Morillon. I don't want to get into a lot of that but just a couple of questions on that. Can you confirm that there were evacuations of -- of Muslim refugees from the Srebrenica area in - I think it was - March, April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure that there were. I am absolutely sure that there were, because as I have already said General Morillon told me that at the Serbian side, in Serbia, at the customs. And I could see the convoy pass by from the window of the municipal building. I didn't go out, I just saw the column of vehicles. The reason why I didn't go out -- or, rather, the reason why I looked out was there was a noise, vehicles passing by. That's what I heard, the vehicles passing by. We asked ourselves, What's happening? We looked out and we saw a convoy of UNHCR trucks with the white -- and nobody notified us officially that it would take place, but we saw it from the wind I. Nobody told us that Morillon had agreed with somebody from the army that a certain number of persons would be evacuated from Srebrenica, and then when we saw the trucks we realised that this was, in fact, going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, and as I've said you talked a fair amount about that. I don't want to get into that details too much. But in a state -- in your state court testimony, in Mitrovic et al, you were asked a question by one of the Defence counsel to make a comparison between the evacuation of the civilians in 1993 that you witnessed and the evacuation of the civilians in 1995 that you witnessed. Can you do that for us?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then and now, and at any other point in time, I can always just tell you the same thing. As far as my memory serves me, I heard from Morillon that there was a great deal of interest, that the trucks were overloaded; and that he found it difficult to control. It was the impossible to control the people getting onto the trucks, that people spent nights to the truck in order to keep their place to leave in the morning, and that in light of this interest he tried to set up another convoy to take more people out. But that our command, or the army at a higher level, did not approve if. And he, in fact, complained to me about that when we talked at the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I think the lawyer in this case is suggesting that there was nothing wrong in the 1993 evacuation and that there was nothing wrong in the 1995 evacuation. Is that your view in terms of force and pushing and threats and that sort of thing and fear?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people were jostling for position to get onto the trucks. There was even a rumor that the authorities in Srebrenica were trying to prevent people from getting on and that there were fights, fist-cuffs and that with tragic consequences that the trucks were overloaded. I am just telling you what I heard. I don't know the dates. But this is quite unsubstantiated but, but I heard that some people died of affixation or because they were ill, but this is just rumor. Just speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having heard the witness's answer, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a transcript correction which I think should be there now. Page 52, line 7, that the "military authorities," that word was missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, for that. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would like to show you a short video clip on that topic, very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 3841, excuse me. And this is a short clip from the BBC that has been identified to us as being this evacuation. Just a small segment of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So just watch this if you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "Reporter: In trying to do what it thinks best for the people of Srebrenica, the UN has spent more time planning, looking around, being turned back and forth constantly by both sides than actually moving refugees out. It believes that the population of the besieged town should be reduced. Particularly those who are already refugees. The thousands who have no real accommodation or support in the town. And on this basis, the high commissioner for refugees special envoy denies being involved with the policy of ethnic cleansing. "Interviewee: The people we are evacuating from Srebrenica have already been ethnically cleansed because they are coming from areas of --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we stop. I am not sure whether the witness is hearing the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear the interpretation. There was no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was no transcript into B/C/S as transcripts have not been provided to the interpretation booths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that's an important point, Mr. President. The images themselves, I think, are undisputedably admissible. I believe narrative may not be admissible. So it might be best, actually, if the witness doesn't hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's rather a procedural matter than the admissibility itself, but whether the witness can answer the question without having heard the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the English overlay helps put this in contest for the Court. It's nothing that I am asking the witness about. I just want to see the pictures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So can we move -- can we move on without the audio? It's difficult. Okay. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We should be able to, actually. We did it in the last one. If we put -- I think we know what went wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long would you like to stay in 1993, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a fraction of the time in the record, Mr. President, and this is my last one or two questions, and it's going to be well below my two-hour estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, I think we are above the two hours now, but I stand to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 1 hour and 40 minutes. If we could try to play this thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I am not asking you about those -- those military vehicles. Do those shots of refugees look like what it was in 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely how Morillon described the situation in Srebrenica to me. And I can see now, this is the first time that I see this footage. I think that he created the same picture in my mind when he told me what this looked like about trying to get a place in the trucks and that the trucks were overloaded and that he could have taken several such convoys out had the military authorities in the town permitted him to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you've stated that you heard the rumors about people dying on these convoys, and you said these are just rumors. You don't leave them, I take it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's possible because you can see that the trucks were overloaded and that people of ill-health might have died because of stress or cold having spent the whole night there, for instance. You know that in Bratunac there was a strange death 20 days ago or so in ideal conditions at a wedding. So it is to be expected that something like that my occur in a situation like this. I don't think that anyone killed someone else, but people were getting on without any health checks or anything; so those who were ill may have needed medical assistance a long time ago and they were unable to deal with the difficult situation because of the cold and the road to Tuzla is very bad, in particular from the Ljubovija bridge to Drinjaca. That's a macadam road, and I think that they took that route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So when this happened, in 1993, Ljubisa Borovcanin the accused in this case was the commander of the police station in Bratunac, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so. According to the documents that's what he should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you were there. Give us a straight answer, please. Was or was he not the commander of the police at this time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where do you think I was, in Bratunac? Yes. I was, and I do believe that Ljubisa Borovcanin was the police komandir. Please, believe me, I never was interested in those things, who was the komandir, who was the chief, all I was interested in was the policemen, their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Gosnell. Unlike usual sitting, we will take a break at five past 12.00 today, and we will have a half an hour break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will do my best to be done by then, but I can't make any guarantees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you've testified that you don't remember precisely when it was that Mr. Borovcanin left Bratunac to take up a position elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But let me ask you, do you recall -- was it during the year 1994?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to believe me. In my first testimony here, I said that the dates were my weak point, and I am completely unreliable when it comes to dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have P2857, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: PT?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please enlarge this because it's not really legible. Fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me know when you have finished reading the document, sir.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, would it accord with the recollection that you do have, would it be consistent with whatever recollection that you do have, that Mr. Borovcanin would have left to take up his responsibilities elsewhere around this date?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I recall is that Ljubisa Borovcanin left, but I really can't be certain at all. I told you that I had problems with numbers and I cannot guarantee that this is when it happened. I merely heard that I -- I merely remember that I heard somebody tell me that Ljubisa Borovcanin went away to take up some other post, so I can't really sit here and say this is when it happened. I can't be certain it was 1994. I'm sorry that I can't help you about the dates and the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this would have been one week of the minutes of the meeting at which the Prosecution suggested that Mr. Borovcanin became a member of the SDS; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what follows from the documents that we looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have P3840 brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You've already been shown this document, sir. And I point to you again to item 7 -- 7 and 8. Now, you recall you were shown some minutes at an earlier time by the Prosecutor, those minutes were dated the 10th of February, 1993, concerning a proposal for Mr. Borovcanin to become chief of the SJB. Now, again that was back on the 10th of February, 1993. Looking at this document, you can see that Mr. Bogdanovic continues to be the chief of the Bratunac MUP and that Mr. Borovcanin is the komandir; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that this initiative of ours of the municipality -- municipal assembly and the board from Bratunac did not bear fruit and that Luka Bogdanovic remained there for longer than we expected at that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So this would confirm your recollection of the matter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that and that's why I said that our decision may be taken into account, but it doesn't have to necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right, sir. Thank you. Would you please read paragraph 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The above mentioned persons ..." that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could read aloud?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The above mentioned persons are obliged to report to the duty officer at the reception, inform him who they want to see in the command, and ask whether that command member is present in the command, or the headquarters, and if that command member is not present in the headquarters they must say what other person they want to see, and if that person is not there there is no need for the above-mentioned persons to enter the command -- the headquarters at all."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you are sir, is one of the above mentioned persons, did you indeed have to go through this procedure as you entered?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This paper was in the possession of the duty officer at the reception, at the gate; and he was duty-bound to follow the procedure, whether he liked it or not, and so was I.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I thank you, for that, sir. I would like to now move on to another answer that you gave earlier this morning. And in response to a question, you -- from the Prosecution, you said that you saw an encounter on videotape or on television between Mr. Borovcanin -- Well, sir, perhaps I -- do you recall having given an answer about seeing General Mladic on television?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him on TV and I saw him in person up there in Potocari. I saw his address on TV. The address --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the address to the people who were gathered there in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I just want to focus on the -- if you can recognise based on the footage where he was at the time that he was filmed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What person are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he stood in front of the people who had gathered there. They were outside of the DutchBat base.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, the transcript might be interpreted to suggest that there might have been some kind of a meeting between General Mladic and Mr. Borovcanin. I wonder if you would like to the clarify that answer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any meeting between the two. I saw Mr. Borovcanin on TV. He was not there with Mladic, and I am sure that you have the footage because we saw it at least ten times. You can see that from the footage, and I think that all TV channels in Bosnia and Herzegovina broadcast this footage; and I think you can see quite clearly that Borovcanin and Mladic are not there together. And thanks to this footage, I was able to realise that Borovcanin had come to that territory at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we have P3837 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, I would like you to focus on the paragraph above the list of names. And in particular, the portion after the comma which says, and I'll read it: "The republican commissioner, Dr. Dragan Djokanovic, established a war commission for the municipality of Bratunac." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And does that accord with your recollection as to the -- as to who it was who established the commission?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on this and, in fact, I remember when this man came and I knew him from the pre-election campaign, I think that he was at the head of the federalist party; and he was in coalition with Muhamed Filipovic, and Radovan Karadzic when there was this initiative about the survival of Bosnia and Herzegovina or Bosnia and Herzegovina remaining within Yugoslavia. He was one of the advocates of that, so that I knew them from those discussions and obviously he was the commissioner of the president, and he had the powers that if a state of war was declared, I don't know who was in charge of declaring it, the republican assembly, that the members of the war commission would be the following people, whether this was done at the proposal of Djokanovic or the president, I don't know. I don't want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. And one last series of questions to ask you, and it arises out of a question that was asked of you by His Honour Judge Kwon, yesterday, when he asked you or suggested to you that perhaps it would have been likely that you would have indeed attended this meeting with President Karadzic. Now, I just want to ask you a few questions about that. You mention that Mr. Deronjic was president of the SDS in Bratunac and that he was the president of the deputies club of the SDS; isn't that right? In your testimony in Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So does that mean that he was one of the 33 or 35 deputies of the Bratunac assembly as you've also testified?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Leading. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, in a sense it's leading in a sense it's not. All of this is actually on the record in this transcript and from Blagojevic. I'm actually not extending anything that's not already on the record, and I'm just laying a foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll bear that in mind with next question and let's move on with this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I am just trying to lay a foundation for the ultimate question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Point taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So, sir, I'm not sure if you answered the question about what that meant if he was one of the 33 or 35 deputies that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and his vote were just one vote that he could cast for or against in the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did he hold any other position in this Bratunac municipal government?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Apart from when I left the assembly and that post, then he came to replace me because a deputy for a short time --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir -- sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I didn't want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And I should have specified that I was asking the question in relation to July 1995.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1995, he did not have any functions in the municipality apart from the fact that he was the president of the party and the president of the deputies club; and I think he was also a member of the main board at the republican level.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Now you've also testified that in July 1995 Mr. Deronjic was appointed the civil commissioner of Srebrenica by President Karadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I heard that and I think this was also published in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can we -- may we please have P10 put up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, sir, if you can just focus on item 1. Does that accord with your understanding in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw this decision in its entirety, and I never saw up to now until the end what were his authorities and what it actually meant that he had been named as commissioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No, I understand that, sir. I am just asking you about his actual appointment.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I ... yes, this is probably this naming of him to that position, the appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I am informed that the witness used a word other than "probably." I am informed that he used the word "certainly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, can you confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no reason for us not to believe the document which is here. On the basis of the article you can see that it's procedurally ordered; it's a document that I haven't seen to date and it relate to say Miroslav Deronjic and his powers in that period and during that time among other things, you can see. And I recall that he later worked to establish and to institute the authorities in Srebrenica for his further work. Even it is stated here what he will specifically do in Srebrenica afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May we please have P3141.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you can see again from this document, sir, item number 1 or at number 1, we can see the name Miroslav Deronjic and several other names. And the date is July 14th, and it states, "Decision on the appointment of the War Presidency of the Srebrenica-Skelani municipality." Now, I just have one final question for you, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I may have to go back on that assertion, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Having looked at these documents and paced on your knowledge and experience, do you think that Mr. Deronjic may have met Dr. Karadzic as a representative of the Bratunac municipality or in his capacity as the civilian commissioner of the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have met with him only as part of this function or in the capacity that he had been appointed to by the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would request the Court's indulgence for us to take the break now. I would like to opportunity to consult and then close my examination thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. 30 minutes. --- Break taken at 12.06 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, I am back, but Judge Prost has left us and now we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis in another composition. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, a very few brief further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, we left off with the decision on the appointment of the War Presidency of Srebrenica-Skelani municipalities dated 14 July, 1995, listing the appointees to that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I now request that P905 be placed on e-court? P2905.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's still coming up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, you'll see this document. Again, you saw it -- I believe it was shown to you by the Prosecution -- I'm sorry, it was shown to you on cross-examination by the Beara Defence. We see the date there 14 July 1995, the same date as the previous document. And the third line down, you see "+1100, Miroslav Deronjic, and a delegation from Srebrenica." Now, again, based on your knowledge and experience would you understand that a delegation from Srebrenica, as referred to here, would consist of the individuals listed on the decision that you last looked at?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the delegation appointed here wanted to go and speak. Probably in that composition about what and how they will do in Srebrenica, that they needed to set up things because they probably just like myself didn't know exactly how to find their way in that situation giving the circumstances. So it was about the kind of organisation and how it would be done. This is my assumption. I believe that it is quite close to the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I have one last question, for you, sir. Did you ever see Mr. Borovcanin engaging in any activities on behalf of the SDS party, whether before the 17th of February, 1994, or after the 17th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that and -- I mean, these documents were a surprise to me because I never was of the conviction that he was a member appointed, or that he ever did anything as a member. I never heard that he had any kind of appointment by the party. Perhaps this was the first step towards joining and then had he really wanted to be an active member or if he wanted to be the bearer of any function he would probably have had to make some corrections in his official capacities and duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Some clarification. Mr. Simic, I am not sure whether it was yesterday or the day before, to the question put by Mr. Ostojic representing Mr. Beara, whether you had any discussion with Mr. Deronjic as to the Kravica warehouse you heard from somebody else. I think you answered "no." You didn't any discussion with Deronjic at all, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had any conversations or heard the -- the first time I heard of it was when I read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You read what? What do you mean when you read it? You --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some conversation between Deronjic and Karadzic which was shown to me in the course of yesterday, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I am not clear about it. But let me read the part of your testimony given at the Blagojevic trial.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is page 7628 from line 17 and onwards. So this is the time-frame when you heard about the Kravica warehouse, the killing from probably from Davidovic or sometime later on. I quote: "All right, well you did you have a meeting or did you run into Mr. Deronjic after this encounter with Colonel Beara?" I don't know, I think I'm mistaken. It's page 7630 from line 13: "Okay, now when you learned of the Kravica warehouse incident, did you have any discussions with any other members of the government or the SDS president, also the commissioner by now, of civilian affairs, Miroslav Deronjic." And this is what you answered: "I asked why that had happened and whether it could have been avoided. He seemed equally shocked ask taken aback. He seemed to have heard about the incident when it was already too late for anything to be done." So now you remember that part of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I think I asked him that when he came to the assembly to hand over that document from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To certain extent that you had discussion with Deronjic on that matter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just asked him if the thing in Kravica could have been avoided and whether he knew how that came about, because I knew his function at the time, whether he had insight or whether he could have intervened or predicted it in any anyway, whatever. But anyway, as I said he was like that, and he said that he found out about Kravica late when he could no longer do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me clarify one thing further in relation to your encounter with Mr. Beara. After you met with Davidovic, you went into the -- went to the SDS building in front of which you --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- met an officer. And at the time you didn't know who he is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But let me read the part of your testimony at Blagojevic again. It is page 7627 where you said, I quote: "I saw an officer there, a senior officer, whom I know now, for whom I know now is called Beara." You said now you know he is Beara. Could you elaborate on that, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gladly. I accepted that, what I was told and there was no one else except Beara, and I accepted that as such. And I said "Yes, I know." I said yesterday, however, and today, that I am not reliably sure that this is correct, but the person who said that probably had his own reasons why he said that. He must have had some assumption on the basis of which he said that it was him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sometime later on, I take it that you must have seen an image or picture of Mr. Beara, either through TV or newspaper or whatever?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him on television. Whether he surrendered or was arrested I don't remember. And I saw -- at crossings I saw warrants -- or wanted lists, and that's what I saw of him, what he was like at these wanted persons lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Having seen those pictures or images, were you or were you not able to confirm whether it was Mr. Beara that you saw in front of the building on that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are willing, I am willing to try to explain to you why. I had a number of times the opportunity to see people in uniform and out of uniform, and believed me they are very different once they take their uniform off. Their appearance and face and build is entirely different than when they are wearing civilian uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your answer is no. You are not able to confirm whether it was Beara --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No still. And I said yesterday that I wasn't able the confirm this amongst other things because I was not even the concentrated at that time to see who that person was. I wasn't interested to know what he looked like, but what I wanted to know is could he do what I was asking him to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. My final question. When the convoys of buses arrived in Bratunac, you and other people were concerned about them. And at the end of the day, they left?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand in what sense concerned and which convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were you upset or agitated? Were the buses full of the prisoners, and you were concerned about the security of Bratunac, et cetera. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand now which convoy you are thinking of. Yes, that is why I intervened and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Instead of convoy, the buses. But, my point is that at the end of the day the buses left. My question is -- yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is not an objection, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I am not sure whether you are using the vernacular expression "at the end of the day," or whether you actually mean a point and time. I'm a little confused, and I am not sure it might be translated to witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. At that time -- at some point of time during that day, the buses left.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the president of the executive board told me that this was done and they finally left in the direction that the rest of the buses had gone the day before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is whose decision it was to have those buses leave Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably someone from the army command, because they, they, according to them came and left from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you by any chance know, even with hindsight, who it was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who from the army command? I wouldn't be able to say because I don't know who had which duties within the command, so I would not speculate whether it was the duty person who was in charge of that or did somebody order that to them or to him? Well, all I could do is speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Simic -- yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like the record to reflect specifically on page 68 in the answer that the witness gave, although I am not sure I should proceed with him listening, but I'll leave that to you, I think there was a word that the witness used that was consistent with what he said yesterday but was not interpreted and therefore not transcribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you remove your headphones, please, Mr. Simic. And, usher, can you assist him in the way that the headphones are away from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will be using a B/C/S word, so I don't know if it has that great of an impact. And I certainly did not want to object during the Honourable Judge Kwon's questioning. On line 12, I think, when the witness answered by saying, "gladly I accepted that that what I was told," and then he used the word "verovanto," which is probably, which is consistent with what he said yesterday as opposed to the way it reads now omitting that word or even the translated it could be "apparently," but it certainly used the word, "verovanto," so we could either check the video of that, but I think it's consistent with what he said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anybody wishes to comment on that? No. Can you -- you remember when my colleague was referring you to page 7627 of the Blagojevic testimony, of the testimony in Blagojevic. And you said, "Gladly, I accepted that, what I was told," this is what we have in the transcript, "and there was no one else except Beara and I accepted that as such." Did you use the word "probably" in your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, probably. It is probably Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. There are no further questions for you, Mr. Simic, which means you are free to go. Our staff will assist you. On behalf of the Trial Chamber I wish to thank you for having come over, and I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Just 4D606 which includes the two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And subject to the matter that I raised at the beginning, namely, a subsequent filing concerns these three corrections to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, of course, his testimony has already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Formally I am not sure if it's been admitted in the beginning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we admit it. But if we didn't we are admitting it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from the other colleagues? None. So the documents are so admitted. Anyone else from the Defence teams wishes to tender other documents? None. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. 65 ter number 210, minutes of the SDS municipal board. Now, I am told that ERN range is the whole thing because it came in one book, and I don't think we want all that in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't you have the ERN reference for that particular page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will check that. I had used two or three of them and I will get that cleared up for you very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime we know what you are talking about. Is there an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just like to defer a response on that. I haven't had a chance to look at the pages and also look at the transcript more carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that will be MFIed for the time being and then we will decide if we hear any further from you. If we don't hear any further from you, we will proceed with having them admitted. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then number 3837, that was the appointment of the commission, the war commission, of 1992. That was the one that was in the name of the witness. And then 3838, that was the Bratunac Brigade report about establishing military rule on December 30th, 1992. And then 3840, that is another Bratunac Brigade order about the list of people coming into reception. And then 3841, the video clip of -- just the short video clip of some of the evacuations from 1993. And counsel had objected to the time of the overlay, the BBC commentary. It wasn't meant for the commentary, so I think it could go in either way. So we don't need the commentary if there is an objection. But I would like the images because he testified a lot about the images and that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, if it's all the same to my learned friend, the opposite, we do object to the commentary, but the images are completely fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to clarify it, that's a big video, but the clips that we played were 1355 to 1510, and I will get to the ERNs for those other documents. Just from the English version, Mr. President, the SDS municipal board of February 1993 is 0219 through 2709 to 2805. And that's just in the English a 4-page document, 18 through 21. And the next one was the meeting from the minutes held in January 1994. The English ERN is 0219 through 2709 to 2805, 41, page 41 through 44 in the English. And then I think at the last set of meetings I had was the February SDS municipal board meeting, which was 0219-2709 through 2805, and that's page 45, 46, 47, 48 -- through 49, basically. And we don't need the rest of those minutes from all the other years. So it's just these three sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, that's a lot to digest. I would just like to reserve our position and come back to you if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Monday, Monday. Thank you. Next witness. Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Jankovic, and welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are about to start giving evidence as a Defence witness for the Defence team of Mr. Borovcanin. Before you do so you need to mange a solemn declaration that you, in the course of your testimony you will be speaking truth. Text is going to be handed to you now, please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn commitment with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Lazarevic will go first. We won't finish your testimony today because we have only got less -- a little bit more than half an hour. We will continue on Monday, tomorrow being a UN holiday we won't have any sitting. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me introduce myself to you for the record, although we have had an opportunity to meet. My name is Aleksandar Lazarevic, and together with my colleagues I represent Mr. Borovcanin before this Tribunal. Before I begin asking you questions, I would just like to warn you. We speak the same language, and could you please wait for me to finish my question and then start making your answer so that we can avoid the overlap which creates problems for the interpreters. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Now, I would like you to state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Could you now tell us when and where you were born?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 15th of September, 1967, in Vranjak, Modrica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Could you please tell me something about your education, did you complete it in your place of birth, did you go and get an education somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I completed the elementary school in Vranjak, and secondary school I attended in Sarajevo. It was the school of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me when it was, what year did you graduate from this school of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the school in 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, where did you live up until the time when the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: After I graduated from the secondary school, I started working in Modrica as a policeman. I started at my job on the 1st of July, 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you to speak up a little bit or to get a little bit closer to the microphones. So I conclude on the basis of what you've just told us that you live in Modrica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I lived in Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And you told us that you started with your job in the police. Could you please tell me whether right from the start you started working in the police whether there were any changes in terms of your employment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as I graduated from the school I started working in the police and I never did anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell us, briefly, about your career in the police. What kind of work did you do at the beginning, did you then move to some other tasks within the police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was first a beat officer, patrolling the area. And for a period I worked in Sarajevo in the republican secretariat of the interior. For a while I was providing security to persons and facilities and for a period of time I was -- I worked on trains, providing security on trains, and then I went on to do the work of a traffic policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me whether you are employed now?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I am unemployed. I am retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on now to 1995. Let's start from the beginning. Could you please tell me what duties did you have in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, I was a traffic policeman in the traffic police station in Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you a few questions about your regular police work in 1995. Could you tell me, what kind of uniform did you wear at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time we had blue uniforms. We, the traffic policemen, had white sleeve covers and white hats on top of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. And could you please tell me while you did your regular police work as a traffic policeman, did you carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had our sidearms, a pistol in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Now, I would like you to explain to us very briefly the structure. I will go through it with you through my questions so that people could see what the traffic police station looked like, what its structure was. Could you tell me, who was your superior in situations where you performed your regular police work?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the commander, "komandir," and his deputy. They were my superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We are now talking about traffic police station in Modrica. In terms of the chain of command, who was superior to the komandir and the deputy komandir of the traffic police station?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be the chief of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Could you please tell me, I have a question in relation to this. In July 1995, did you perhaps have some kind of a rank?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We did not have ranks up until 1995. We had our functional designations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Well, in addition to the regular police work that we've just talked about, were you a member of the PJPs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of a PJP of the Doboj public security centre. That also included members of my police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think that at page 78, line 16, there is a correction for the transcript. When you were talking about this you said at that time, and I was asking you about 1995, you said that you had functional designations, you meant that you didn't have ranks. That's what you said? I don't want to put words into your mouth but that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that in 1995 there were no ranks in the police. There were just functional designations or insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So before I took you back to the previous question you were telling us about being a member of the PJPs in the Doboj public security centre, or, rather, that personnel from your station went to those PJPs. Can you please tell me, based on your recollection, those PJPs, in what public security centre were they formed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Each public security centre had its PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific now. You mentioned -- or, rather, can you tell us what centre did your PJP belong to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: My unit, the unit that I belonged to was under the public security centre in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Could you now tell me, to the best of your recollection, how many companies of the PJP were there in the Doboj public security centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: A total of five companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What company did you belong to, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I belonged to the 5th Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have to go through all this? Can't we go straight to the facts that really he is here to testify upon? The facts in July, 1995, when he was captured?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understand your suggestion; however, what I want to establish, maybe it's not appropriate to say this in front of the witness. But there were some important issues in relation to PJP Doboj and the companies, this is why I am -- have to go through this, because there were some suggestions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I didn't see those in the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Then I have -- I apologise, this is just a foundational issue to explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, could you please tell me in the 5th PJP company who was the commander of your company?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 5th PJP company was Milan Gavric from Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me who was the deputy commander of the PJP company, the 5th PJP company that you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The deputy commander was the commander of the 1st Platoon, Zeljko Puseljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have some kind of a function in the 5th PJP company from the Doboj public security centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the commander of the 3rd Platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I just have a couple of more questions on this topic. Could you please tell me whether your PJP company included only personnel of the public security station from Modrica or did it include personnel from other public security stations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: There were other personnel from other stations, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me what other public security stations provided staff for your PJP company?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Our PJP company got the personnel from Doboj Derventa, Vukosavlje Brod, public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. And all those public security stations that you just listed, were they all territorially under the Doboj public security centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in Doboj there was a special police detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a special police detachment in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like us to clear some things for your further testimony. This special police detachment, was it functionally apart from the PJPs and the regular police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that detachment was in the Doboj public security centre, physically, but in terms of its chain of command it was not part of it. The chief of the centre could not exercise command over this detachment. They were subordinated to the special police brigade and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. I just have a small correction for the transcript. You were, of course, talking about the fact that it was territorially in Doboj, because it -- it is stated here that it was physically in the Doboj public security centre, what you meant is that it was territorially in the Doboj public security centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Its headquarters were in Doboj, in the town of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, I think that now it is clear. To clear this up, let me ask you this: The commander of the special police detachment from Doboj, could he issue orders to you or to any other member of the public security station in Modrica, in Doboj, whatever?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, they could not issue any orders to us. They could, perhaps, ask us to provide assistance to them, but they -- we couldn't issue orders to them, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Now, I would like us to pursue this topic of the PJPs. As a member of the PJP, when you went into the field, did you wear the same uniform that you had when you performed your regular police work or was it different?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: We did not have the same uniforms. We had special uniform we wore when we went out to do those tasks. It was a camouflage green uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. And could you tell me when you went out to do those tasks, when you were involved in the working of the PJPs, what kind of weapons did you have? The same kind of official pistols that you carried when you went about your regular police work?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not carry pistols. We had automatic weapons, automatic rifles, and as far as I can recall in my platoon there were three light machine-guns, 7.62 millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Apart from what you've just told us, did any members of the PJP company have any heavier weapons, larger calibre?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When you took part in operations as a member of the PJP, did you have any communication equipment that you could use to communicate with each other?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We would usually get those once we were in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what kind of communication equipment are we talking about that you were issued once you were in the field?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Those were small Motorolas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now tell me, to the best of your recollection, your PJP company, how many of those Motorolas did it receive?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: We were issued with four Motorolas. One was kept by the company commander, and the three platoon commander each had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. And just a few questions on this topic. When your company, the 5th PJP Company from the Zvornik public security centre, did it have a medical team which would intervene if any of you got wounded in the course of combat and treat the wounded?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think you've just made a mistake when you said the Zvornik PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes, it's possible. What I meant was the PJP company from Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The PJP from Doboj did not have a medical team.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you now whether you had a logistics platoon within your company that would make sure that you had ammunition, supplies, combat equipment, food, was there anything like that in your company?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, we did not have anything of the sort in our company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now tell me, when you went into combat what -- how did you receive ammunition supplies, materiel, food, and all the other stuff that you needed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: We received all this from whoever it was that we were subordinated in the field, and usually those were army units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions before we move on to specific events from 1992. Can you please tell us whether there was a mortar squad or an artillery section in your unit that could provide fire support in combat?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't have going like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me now when you would go out in the field when you went with your company out in combat, what sort of transport vehicles were available to you? How were you taken to these places where your engagement was required?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Usually, we would rent buses from some transport company for the purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't have your own bus, but the buses were rented; is that correct? Did I understand your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't have our own buses. They were rented from other companies, transport companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions on this topic. When you would go in the field for combat, you said that you were already -- you already said that you were in traffic and transport police, did you use the blue and white police vehicles with rotation lights -- rotating lights or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't use those vehicles for combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of more questions on this. Before July 1995, did you take part in any combat as a member of the PJP of the Doboj centre?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did participate on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. I am not going to spend too much time on this. What I am interested in is this: How did you receive the information, for example, today you are performing your regular task, you are overseeing traffic, how would you receive information that you would need to go to the PJP and that you were being sent to a different kind of assignment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I would be informed about that by my superiors, usually orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I would like to move to July 1995 and to events relating to Srebrenica. Can you please tell me, you personally, when did you find out for the first time that the VRS forces had entered Srebrenica? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this was on the 12th of July. And I found out from the media, this was in the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. And can you please tell me in your best recollection, how did you receive information that you were supposed to report to the PJP in Modrica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I received the notification on the 13th, around noon, approximately, around 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall who informed you about this? How did you receive this notification that you were supposed to assemble?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I was informed about it by the deputy komandir of my station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: After you received this notification, you left. Can you just briefly tell me how this assembling of the PJP members from Modrica proceeded on that day? Where did you assemble? How many of you turned up? Did you bring your equipment with you? Can you please tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: We assembled in front of the Modrica police station. Usually members of my station would come there, and that's how it was this time as well. After that, we went to the intersection not far from the town centre, the intersection is called Jakesnica. We would wait for the buses there that came from Doboj -- the direction of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me just put a sub-question to you. How many of you were there from the Modrica police station? How many of you assembled in front of the police station and then proceeded to the Jakesnica intersection?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not really quite sure, but I believe it was between 10 and 15 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I am not surely going to the insist on you providing the exactly number, but can you please tell me did you take your weapons with you? And if you did, what did you take with you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: We took our automatic weapons and one combat kit of ammunition each, as well as dry rations for one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I just want to ask you at the time when you gathered in front of the police station in Modrica, can you tell me if you were told where you would be going?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: We were told that we were going to Zvornik and that we would receive further information -- or further instructions once we reached Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I interrupted you at one point with some follow-up questions, so members of the Modrica police station came to the Jakesnica intersection, and then can you tell us what happened after that? How was this trip unfolding, what happened?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Two buses from the direction of Doboj came to the Jakesnica intersection, we boarded the second bus because the first one was already full and the company commander Gavric was already on that bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but in order for us to have a clear answer, was Gavric in the first bus or in the second bus where you were?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Gavric and I were not on the same bus, Gavric was in the first bus and I was in the second bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. I think that is clear now. And tell me, in your estimate, how many of you were in the two buses that went in the direction of Zvornik, a total number?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The two buses were full, so it was about 100 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... start with some documents and if we can adjourn earlier, five minutes earlier today, because it's a completely different topic and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, we are going to the finish here today. We will continue on Monday as I explained to you because tomorrow is a UN holiday, and we won't have a sitting. Between now and Monday you have an obligation not to communicate with anyone here or in your country in connection with the matters that you are testifying upon. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Has someone explained to you this obligation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was explained to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Victims and Witnesses Section explained it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank the witnesses and victims section for doing that regularly with all witnesses, but I just wanted to make sure the witnesses understand. So we stand adjourned thank you and have nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
